messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling and urban environment
parts:
Marco

There are considerable challenges when trying to use line transect sampling in an urban environment.  Detectability is not strictly a function of distance as some birds will be on rooftops and invisible even at close distances.

Also, the transects cannot be randomly placed.  You will be forced to travel along streets, and you cannot travel through buildings; leading to non-random sampling.

Yet another challenge:  Distance sampling assumes that density of animals is the same at all distances from the transect; stated another way, animals are distributed independently of the transect.  This is the so-called "design assumption" Buckland et al. (2015) Section 1.7

If you examine the one paper on distance sampling of urban pigeons (Giunchi et al. 2007, http://eprints.adm.unipi.it/521/1/Article_cat.pdf) you will see an absence of detections close to the transect.  The cause of this is not that detectability was difficult, but rather because pigeons were unlikely to rest in the middle of the streets used as transects by these investigators.

They employed left-truncation which is a remedy that does not directly address the issue of non-uniform distribution with respect to the transect.

It is difficult to adequately sample habitats in an urban environment, whether it be for pigeons or feral dogs and cats.
